analysis.one_liner: Barred health insurers from using genetic information to deny coverage or raise premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in April 1996 and died there without ever receiving a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to deny coverage, cancel policies, or charge higher premiums based on a person's genetic information — including information about family members who share their bloodline. It also would have stopped insurers from demanding genetic test results and from sharing them without a person's written permission. The bill never left its Senate committee and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with genetic risk factors — for example, someone whose parent carried a gene linked to breast cancer or Huntington's disease — would have been protected from being priced out of coverage or refused insurance for a condition they do not yet have and may never develop. People considering genetic testing would have been able to get tested without fear that the result could be used against them or their relatives.

how_it_helps.text: Insurance providers could not deny or cancel coverage, or vary premiums and terms, based on genetic information or on a person having requested or received genetic services [S2] [S3].
Insurers could not require applicants or enrollees to disclose genetic information, and could not disclose such information without prior written authorization for each disclosure [S2] [S3].

People could enforce the protections themselves through a private right of action, including injunctions and monetary damages, alongside enforcement by state insurance commissioners and the Secretary of Labor for employer plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose the ability to price individual policies using genetic risk information, and the costs of covering people with genetic risk would spread across the broader insurance pool in the form of somewhat higher premiums for everyone. Employer plans would face federal enforcement under existing pension-law machinery.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and the wider premium pool

drawbacks.text: By barring insurers from pricing genetic risk, the bill would shift expected costs from individuals with genetic risk onto the whole premium pool, which insurers argue would raise premiums for everyone else [S3].

The bill expressly did not require any group or employee health plan to provide particular benefits, so a person protected from genetic discrimination still had no guarantee of coverage for the care they need [S3].

Enforcement was split between state insurance commissioners for most policies and the Secretary of Labor for employer plans, and the new private right of action invited litigation over what counts as 'genetic information' [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — that a healthy person cannot be penalized for DNA they were born with — is a real protection that matters most to people with serious family histories of disease. The cost is that insurers, unable to price that risk, would spread it across premiums, and the bill left the underlying problems of coverage and benefit guarantees untouched. It was a targeted civil-rights-style fix, not a comprehensive answer to insurance affordability.

outcome.mechanism: It was read in the Senate and sent to the Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on April 23, 1996 [S5] [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill sat there through the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997, and never reached the Senate floor [S5] [S1].
The bill drew only one cosponsor over its entire life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: they kept the ability to consider genetic information in underwriting, and people with genetic risk never got the protection this bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; no chairman scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican senator with one Democratic cosponsor, so it was bipartisan in form but drew almost no visible support from either party.

industries.note: Because the bill died, insurers kept the freedom to deny, cancel, or reprice coverage based on genetic information and to request genetic test results. That freedom is precisely what people with inherited disease risk feared, and it persisted for years after this bill failed.

industries.industry: Genetic testing and genetic counseling services
industries.note: The bill would have protected people who request or receive genetic services from insurance consequences, likely making patients more willing to get tested and counseled. With the bill dead, fear of insurance discrimination could deter people from seeking those services.
